rows.question: When does my maternity leave start if my due date is 15 November 2026?
rows.reply:
Under Mutterschutz (statutory maternity protection period) rules, the protection period before birth covers the last six weeks before the expected date of delivery. Your employer may not employ you during this time, unless you expressly declare that you are willing to work ("soweit sie sich nicht zur Arbeitsleistung ausdrücklich bereit erklärt"). You can withdraw that declaration at any time, with effect for the future.

The period is counted from the expected delivery date shown on the certificate from your doctor, midwife or male midwife ("Entbindungspfleger"). Counting six weeks back from 15 November 2026 gives 4 October 2026. If the baby is not born on the expected date, the period before birth becomes shorter or longer to match.

After the birth, your employer may not employ you until eight weeks have passed. This extends to twelve weeks in three cases:
1. premature births ("Frühgeburten");
2. multiple births ("Mehrlingsgeburten");
3. where a disability of the child within the meaning of § 2(1) sentence 1 SGB IX is medically confirmed before the eight weeks end. This third extension applies only if you apply for it.

If the baby is born early, the period after birth is also extended by the time lost from the period before birth. The twelve-week extension does not apply to a stillbirth.

Maternity pay (Mutterschaftsgeld) under SGB V §24i is paid for these protection periods and for the day of delivery. For payment before the birth, the decisive document is the doctor's or midwife's certificate stating the expected delivery date.

rows.question: How long after birth can we apply for Elterngeld without losing money?
rows.reply:
The law does not set an application deadline for Elterngeld (parental allowance). It limits how far back payment reaches, and that is where money can be lost.

BEEG §7(1) says Elterngeld is paid retroactively only for the last three months of the child's life before the start of the month of life in which the application is received: "rückwirkend nur für die letzten drei Lebensmonate vor Beginn des Lebensmonats geleistet, in dem der Antrag auf Elterngeld eingegangen ist." Months of the child's life earlier than those three are not paid. The point that counts is when the application is received, not when it is sent.

The months counted are months of the child's life, not calendar months. Elterngeld can be received from the day of birth and is paid in monthly amounts for the child's months of life (BEEG §4(1) and (2)). The same paragraph of §4 limits how long it can be received: Basiselterngeld until the child completes the 14th month of life, and Elterngeld Plus until the 32nd month of life, provided that from the 15th month it is taken in consecutive months by at least one parent. For children born early, §4(5) extends the Basiselterngeld period to the 15th, 16th, 17th or 18th month of life, depending on whether the child was born at least six, eight, twelve or sixteen weeks before the expected date of delivery.

The application must be made in writing ("schriftlich zu beantragen", §7(1)). If you later change the choices made in it, the same three-month limit applies: a change can be made retroactively only for the last three months of life before the start of the month in which the change request is received (§7(2)).

Your local Elterngeld office decides each application and which months are paid.

rows.question: How much notice do I have to give my employer for Elternzeit?
rows.reply:
Elternzeit (parental leave (unpaid job-protected leave)) is requested from your employer in writing, and the minimum notice depends on when the leave falls (BEEG §16(1)).

- Leave up to the child's third birthday: at least seven weeks before the leave begins ("spätestens sieben Wochen").
- Leave between the third birthday and the end of the child's eighth year: at least 13 weeks before it begins ("spätestens 13 Wochen").

The request must be made "in Textform". The Familienportal explains that this includes a letter without a signature or an email.

Other rules in the same section:

- If you request leave falling before the third birthday, you must also state which periods within two years you will take leave ("für welche Zeiten innerhalb von zwei Jahren").
- For urgent reasons, an appropriate shorter notice period is possible as an exception ("Bei dringenden Gründen ist ausnahmsweise eine angemessene kürzere Frist möglich"). The Familienportal gives premature births, or an adoptive placement that could not be planned in time, as examples. It says the notice that then applies depends on the individual case.
- If a mother takes leave straight after the maternity protection period, that period counts towards the two-year period. If she takes annual leave between the two, that annual leave counts too.
- If a mother cannot request leave in time, for a reason that is not her fault, she may make the request within one week after that reason ends (BEEG §16(2)). This applies only to leave directly after the maternity protection period.
- Each parent may split the leave into three periods. More periods need the employer's consent.
- Your employer must give you written confirmation of the Elternzeit ("Der Arbeitgeber hat ... die Elternzeit zu bescheinigen").

Protection against dismissal starts once leave has been requested. It begins at the earliest eight weeks before leave up to the third birthday. For leave between the third and eighth birthdays, it begins at the earliest 14 weeks before (BEEG §18(1)).

The Familienportal also says that for births before 1 July 2015 the notice is seven weeks in all cases. The transitional provision behind that statement is not among the excerpts here, so it cannot be confirmed from the statute.

rows.question: How long is maternity protection after the birth if the baby comes early?
rows.reply:
Under the Maternity Protection Act, Mutterschutz (statutory maternity protection period) after the birth is normally eight weeks. The law says the employer may not employ a woman "bis zum Ablauf von acht Wochen nach der Entbindung" (MuSchG §3(2)). If the baby comes early, two separate rules can lengthen this.

1. Any early birth: the six-week period before the birth is calculated from the expected due date. If the birth comes earlier, that period is shortened (§3(1)). The statute then adds the lost days to the period after the birth: "Bei vorzeitiger Entbindung verlängert sich die Schutzfrist nach der Entbindung … um den Zeitraum der Verkürzung der Schutzfrist vor der Entbindung" (§3(2)). The Familienportal explains that the total therefore still comes to 14 weeks. The period after the birth ends as many days after the eight weeks as the baby arrived before the due date.

2. A premature birth in the medical sense (Frühgeburt): the period after the birth is extended to twelve weeks (§3(2)). The days lost before the birth are also added on top of these twelve weeks. The Familienportal gives a birth weight under 2,500 grams as an example of a Frühgeburt. It says that in this case the total period rises from 14 to 18 weeks.

The statute extends the post-birth period to twelve weeks in three cases, not just one:
- "bei Frühgeburten" (premature births);
- "bei Mehrlingsgeburten" (twins, triplets or more);
- where a disability of the child is medically diagnosed before the end of eight weeks after the birth. This third case applies only if the mother applies for it ("nur, wenn die Frau dies beantragt"). The Familienportal says this application is made to the health insurance fund (Krankenkasse).

The twelve-week extension does not apply in the case of a stillbirth ("Satz 2 gilt nicht bei einer Totgeburt").

During the period after the birth, the employer may not employ the mother, and she cannot waive this. The Familienportal calls it an absolute ban on employment. The one exception is for school pupils and students: they may resume training activities if they expressly ask for this, and they can withdraw that request at any time (§3(3)). Maternity pay from the statutory health insurance is paid for the protection period under §3 and for the day of birth (SGB V §24i(3)).

rows.question: Can my employer dismiss me while I am pregnant?
rows.reply:
In general, no. Under Kündigungsschutz (protection against dismissal) in § 17 of the Maternity Protection Act (MuSchG), dismissal of a woman is not permitted ("Die Kündigung gegenüber einer Frau ist unzulässig") in all three of these periods:
1. during her pregnancy;
2. until four months after a miscarriage after the twelfth week of pregnancy;
3. until the end of her protection period after the birth, and in any case for at least four months after the birth.

The protection applies only if the employer knows of the pregnancy, miscarriage or birth when dismissing, or is told within two weeks after the dismissal is received ("innerhalb von zwei Wochen nach Zugang der Kündigung"). Missing the two weeks does no harm if the reason is not the woman's fault and she informs the employer without delay. Familienportal adds that the protection applies even if you did not yet know you were pregnant, but you must already have been pregnant when you received the dismissal. The same rules apply to steps an employer takes to prepare a dismissal.

There is an exception. Under § 17(2) MuSchG, the highest state authority responsible for occupational safety, or a body it designates, may in special cases declare a dismissal permissible. These cases must not be connected with the woman's condition during pregnancy, after a miscarriage or after the birth. Such a dismissal must be in writing and must state the reason. Familienportal gives these as examples of special reasons: the company is insolvent; the business is partly closed; in a small business, it cannot continue without a qualified replacement; or the employee committed a particularly serious breach of duty. The employer must apply in writing to the supervisory authority. Without its approval, the dismissal is invalid.

If you are dismissed without that approval, Familienportal says you must bring a claim before the competent labour court to have the dismissal declared invalid. It says the claim must normally be filed within 3 weeks of receiving the written dismissal ("normalerweise innerhalb von 3 Wochen"). If you do not file a claim, the dismissal is treated as legally effective. You can file the claim yourself or through a representative such as a lawyer. You can also make it orally, recorded by the court registry. Familienportal also says you should involve the competent supervisory authority.

If the authority did approve the dismissal, you can also challenge that approval. Depending on the state, this is done by an objection or by a court claim. This is a separate procedure. It does not replace the claim before the labour court and cannot on its own preserve your employment.

If your contract is fixed-term, Familienportal says maternity protection lasts as long as the contract runs and ends when the contract ends.

If you take parental leave after the birth, protection can continue under § 18 of the Federal Parental Allowance and Parental Leave Act (BEEG). The employer may not dismiss you from the time parental leave is requested. This protection starts at the earliest:
1. 8 weeks before parental leave taken before the child's third birthday;
2. 14 weeks before parental leave taken between the third birthday and the end of the child's eighth year.
The employer also may not dismiss you during parental leave. In special cases, the same state occupational-safety authority can exceptionally declare a dismissal permissible.

Whether a particular dismissal is valid is decided by the labour court. Questions about maternity protection can go to your supervisory authority, which is responsible for enforcing the Maternity Protection Act.

rows.question: Is there an income limit above which we get no Elterngeld?
rows.reply:
Yes. Under federal law there is an income limit above which the claim to Elterngeld (parental allowance) ends.

The rule (BEEG §1(8)): the claim ends ("Ein Anspruch entfällt") if the entitled person had zu versteuerndes Einkommen (taxable income) of more than 175,000 euros in the last completed tax assessment period before the birth ("im letzten abgeschlossenen Veranlagungszeitraum vor der Geburt des Kindes"). The statute defines this as taxable income under § 2 Absatz 5 of the Einkommensteuergesetz.

If another person also meets the conditions of §1(1) sentence 1 no. 2 (living in one household with the child), or of §1(3) or (4), the claim ends instead if the two persons' taxable incomes added together exceed 175,000 euros ("wenn die Summe des zu versteuernden Einkommens beider Personen mehr als 175 000 Euro beträgt").

Taxable income is not gross income. The official Familienportal guidance says gross income is usually considerably higher. Special expenses, pension and insurance contributions, individual allowances and extraordinary burdens are deducted to reach it. Taxable income is set by the Finanzamt and shown in the tax assessment notice (Steuerbescheid). The guidance gives an example: for a married couple without children who are both employed, 175,000 euros of taxable income corresponds to roughly 207,000 euros gross.

Earlier births: the Familienportal guidance says different, higher limits applied to births before the current rule. The statutory transitional provision for earlier births is not among the excerpts I have, so I cannot say which limit governs a particular birth date. The responsible Elterngeld office decides that.

When the tax notice is not yet available: the guidance says the Steuerbescheid for the year before the birth should be attached to the application if it exists. Parents can still apply if it is not yet clear whether the limit is exceeded. Under BEEG §8(2), if the tax notice is missing and the application states the limit will probably not be exceeded, Elterngeld is paid subject to revocation if it turns out the limit was exceeded. Under §8(3) no. 1, if it cannot yet be stated whether the limit is exceeded, the decision on the amount is provisional until proof is provided.

Whether your household is above or below the limit is decided only by the Elterngeld office responsible for your area. Questions about how your taxable income is worked out belong to the Finanzamt or a tax adviser.

rows.question: How many months of Elterngeld can we get in total?
rows.reply:
How many months of Elterngeld (parental allowance) parents can receive depends on which variant they choose, how they split the months, and whether the child was born early. BEEG §4 sets these limits.

The basic allowance (Basiselterngeld)
- Together, the parents are entitled to "zwölf Monatsbeträge Basiselterngeld" (twelve monthly payments).
- They get two further months, called "Partnermonate" (partner months), if one parent's earned income is reduced in two of the child's months of life. This makes 14 in total.
- One parent can receive at most 12 monthly payments of the basic allowance.
- Each parent who claims must take Elterngeld for at least two months of life.
- The basic allowance can be received only up to the end of the child's 14th month of life.

The ElterngeldPlus variant
- Instead of one month of the basic allowance, a parent can take two months of "Elterngeld Plus". The Familienportal puts it this way: ElterngeldPlus can be received twice as long as the basic allowance.
- ElterngeldPlus can be received up to the end of the 32nd month of life. From the 15th month onward, at least one parent must take it in consecutive months.
- The Familienportal adds a consequence: if after the 14th month there is a month in which neither parent receives ElterngeldPlus, none can be received afterwards, even if months remain.

The partnership bonus
- On top of their 12 months, each parent can receive up to four monthly payments of the "Partnerschaftsbonus" under §4b.
- According to the Familienportal, these are additional months of ElterngeldPlus. They are available when both parents work part-time at the same time. They are also available to single parents.

Months that are used up automatically
- A mother's months of life in which she receives maternity benefits count as months in which she draws the basic allowance. The Familienportal names Mutterschaftsgeld as one of these benefits.
- Months in which private insurance pays daily sickness benefit (Krankentagegeld) during maternity protection count the same way.
- If both parents receive the basic allowance in the same month, two months count as used. Both parents may draw it at the same time in only one of the first 12 months of life.
- That limit does not apply in four cases:
  - multiple births;
  - premature births in the sense of §4(5);
  - children with a disability that a doctor has determined;
  - children who trigger a sibling bonus (Geschwisterbonus).

Premature births
The parents' joint entitlement to the basic allowance is higher if the child was born:
1. at least 6 weeks before the expected date of delivery: 13 monthly payments;
2. at least 8 weeks before: 14 monthly payments;
3. at least 12 weeks before: 15 monthly payments;
4. at least 16 weeks before: 16 monthly payments.

In these four cases, other limits move as well:
- One parent's maximum rises to 13, 14, 15 or 16 monthly payments respectively, plus up to four partnership-bonus payments.
- The basic allowance can be received up to the end of the 15th, 16th, 17th or 18th month of life.
- ElterngeldPlus still runs to the 32nd month. It must be taken in consecutive months from the 16th, 17th, 18th or 19th month respectively.
- The expected date of delivery is the one shown in the doctor's or midwife's certificate.

Adopted children
For adopted children, Elterngeld can be received from the day the child is taken in, at the latest until the child's eighth birthday.

Which of these rules applies to your family, and how many months you will actually receive, is decided by the Elterngeld office responsible for your district.

rows.question: What is the Partnerschaftsbonus and who qualifies?
rows.reply:
What it is: Under BEEG §4b(1), the Partnerschaftsbonus (partnership bonus months) gives each parent an additional monthly amount of the 'Plus' variant of parental allowance for a month of the child's life ("zusätzlichen Monatsbetrag Elterngeld Plus"). It applies when both parents meet two conditions:
1. Both work at least 24 and at most 32 hours a week, averaged over that month of the child's life ("nicht weniger als 24 und nicht mehr als 32 Wochenstunden im Durchschnitt des Lebensmonats").
2. Both meet the general conditions for parental allowance in BEEG §1.

The official guidance adds that you do not have to work 24 to 32 hours in every single week. What counts is the monthly average.

How long: Each parent can receive at most four bonus months and at least two (§4b(2)). Both parents must take it at the same time and in consecutive months (§4b(3): "nur gleichzeitig und in aufeinander folgenden Lebensmonaten"). §4(4) confirms that a parent can receive up to 12 months of basic parental allowance plus up to four bonus months. For premature births under §4(5), the basic months rise to 13, 14, 15 or 16, and the four bonus months are still added on top. The guidance says you can use the bonus before, between or after your other parental allowance months, including if you otherwise receive only basic parental allowance.

If hours change: §4b(5) says the consecutive-months requirement still counts as met if it later turns out that the conditions were not met in every month applied for. The guidance gives these consequences:
- You must report it to the parental allowance office if your average hours differ from what you planned.
- Any month in which either parent worked under 24 or over 32 hours must be repaid, and both parents lose the bonus for that month.
- Other months are not affected if the conditions were met in at least two months. The payment for those months is kept and not reclaimed.

Separated parents and single parents: The guidance says separated parents can also receive the bonus. A single parent can use it alone, and then only that parent needs to work 24 to 32 hours. In the statute, this sole use is set by §4c(2). A parent who meets one of the grounds in §4c(1) Nos. 1 to 3, and who works 24 to 32 hours a week on average in two to four consecutive months, receives additional monthly amounts of the 'Plus' variant for those months. The three grounds are:
1. The parent meets the conditions for the single-parent tax relief under §24b(1) and (3) of the Income Tax Act, and the other parent lives neither with them nor with the child.
2. Care by the other parent would endanger the child's welfare within the meaning of §1666(1) and (2) of the Civil Code.
3. Care by the other parent is impossible, in particular because of serious illness or severe disability. Economic reasons and being busy with other activities do not count.

Under §4b(4), if one of these grounds arises while the bonus is already being drawn, one parent can continue it under §4c(2).

Amount: The guidance says the bonus is calculated the same way as the 'Plus' variant. It is between 150 and 900 euros per parent per month, depending on income before the birth. Supplements are possible, for example for twins or older siblings. These amounts come from the guidance page, not the statute, and no check date is given in the excerpt, so confirm them with the parental allowance office.

Earlier rules:
- BEEG §27(3) was a pandemic rule. Where bonus months fell wholly or partly before 23 September 2022 and the conditions could not be met because of COVID-19, the income and working hours stated credibly in the application were used instead.
- §27(2) also allowed the bonus to be postponed if only one parent worked in a systemically relevant job.
- The guidance says its explanations apply to children born after August 2021. Partly different rules apply for children born before 1 September 2021.

Whether you qualify, and for how much, is decided only by the parental allowance office responsible for your district. Apply to that office.

rows.question: We forgot to apply for Kindergeld. How far back will they pay?
rows.reply:
Kindergeld (child benefit) is paid backdated for at most six months. The law says payment is made retroactively "nur für die letzten sechs Monate vor Beginn des Monats, in dem der Antrag auf Kindergeld eingegangen ist": only for the last six months before the start of the month in which the application is received. The same provision says the entitlement itself is not affected by this limit ("Der Anspruch auf Kindergeld nach § 62 bleibt von dieser Auszahlungsbeschränkung unberührt"). The limit applies to how far back payment goes, not to whether the entitlement exists. This is not described as an application deadline. The consequence of applying late is that the earlier months are lost.

The official family portal adds two points. Backdated payment requires that Kindergeld was due to you but not paid, for example because no application was made. In the application, state that you are applying retroactively and from when you want to receive Kindergeld.

The application must be made in writing ("schriftlich zu beantragen"), and the portal says it can be made electronically or on paper. Submit it to the Familienkasse at your Agentur für Arbeit. That office decides your application and which months are paid.

rows.question: How much Kindergeld do we get per month for our first child?
rows.reply:
The law sets one monthly amount for every child, including a first child. Both the Einkommensteuergesetz and the Bundeskindergeldgesetz state: "Das Kindergeld beträgt monatlich für jedes Kind 259 Euro" (Kindergeld (child benefit) is 259 euros per month for each child). The amount does not differ by birth order. If the tax-free child allowances are raised, Kindergeld is increased to match, rounded to full euros.

Kindergeld is paid monthly. Payment runs from the start of the month in which the conditions are met to the end of the month in which they stop being met. A child born on 25 May brings the full Kindergeld for May.

During the year, parents first receive Kindergeld. In the annual income tax assessment, the tax office automatically checks whether the tax-free child allowances or the Kindergeld paid are more favourable. No application is needed for this check.

Whether your family is entitled is decided by the Familienkasse, not by this service. The application can be made online with the Bundesagentur für Arbeit.

rows.question: How quickly do we have to register the birth at the Standesamt?
rows.reply:
The birth must be reported to the Standesamt (civil registry office) for the place where the child was born within one week. The statute says the birth is to be reported "binnen einer Woche" (within one week) to the Standesamt "in dessen Zuständigkeitsbereich es geboren ist" (in whose area the child was born). If a child is stillborn, the report must be made "spätestens am dritten auf die Geburt folgenden Werktag", meaning no later than the third working day after the birth.

The law sets out two ways a birth is reported:
- by the persons named in § 19 of the Personenstandsgesetz, orally or in writing. A person reporting this way must substantiate the birth ("glaubhaft zu machen").
- by the institutions named in § 20, in writing.

The federal family portal explains how this works in practice. If your child is born in a hospital, birth centre or maternity clinic, the institution notifies the Standesamt and sends the birth certificate issued at the birth. If your child is born at home, the midwife or doctor issues that certificate, and you must present it to the Standesamt within one week.

The federal portal's checklist gives the period as "7 Werktagen" (7 working days). The statute says "binnen einer Woche" (within one week), and the statute governs.

The Standesamt issues the birth certificate. It also passes the registration on to the residents' registration office automatically. For a list of the documents to bring, the portal points to the website of the Standesamt in the place where your child is born.

rows.question: What do we need to bring to the Standesamt to register the birth?
rows.reply:
The federal rule is PStV §33. It says that when a birth is reported, the Standesamt (civil registry office) should ask you to present the following.

1. If the parents are married to each other: your marriage certificate or a certified extract from the marriage register. You also need your own birth certificates if the marriage certificate does not show the registration details of your births. The marriage certificate must be presented even if the marriage has ended.
2. If the parents are not married to each other: the mother's birth certificate. If paternity has already been acknowledged, also the paternity declarations, the father's birth certificate and, where applicable, the joint custody declarations.
3. An identity card, passport or other recognised passport substitute for the parents.
4. If the birth is reported orally: a certificate of the birth issued by a doctor or midwife who was present at the birth.

The Standesamt can also ask for further documents where they are needed to prove the information given ("Das Standesamt kann die Vorlage weiterer Urkunden verlangen").

If you are foreign parents, PStV §34(1) adds a step. When the birth is reported, the Standesamt asks whether a parent holds an unlimited right of residence ("unbefristetes Aufenthaltsrecht"). It also asks whether a parent who is a Swiss citizen, or a family member of one, holds a residence permit under the 1999 EU–Switzerland free movement agreement. This information lets the office check whether the child acquired German citizenship at birth under StAG §4(3). Under PStV §34(2), the Standesamt then asks the foreigners' authority in writing to confirm this. That authority also confirms whether the parent had lived lawfully and habitually in Germany for five years at the time of the birth. The Standesamt decides the result (PStV §34(3)).

The birth certificate from the hospital is handled for you. The Familienportal says that if your child was born in a hospital, birth centre or maternity clinic, the facility notifies the Standesamt and sends the birth certificate. For a home birth, the midwife or doctor issues it, and you must present it to the Standesamt within one week. The Familienportal says the birth must be registered within one week at the Standesamt for the place of birth. Its checklist page says within 7 working days.

For any further documents, the Familienportal points you to the website of the Standesamt in the town where your child is born. That Standesamt decides which documents it requires in your case.

rows.question: Does my Krankenkasse pay for a midwife?
rows.reply:
Yes. Under federal law, a woman insured with a Krankenkasse (statutory health insurer) is entitled to support from a Hebamme (midwife).

SGB V §24d sets out what this covers. The insured woman is entitled to midwife help during pregnancy, at the birth and after the birth. This includes the examinations to confirm the pregnancy and prenatal check-ups ("einschließlich der Untersuchungen zur Feststellung der Schwangerschaft und zur Schwangerenvorsorge").

There is a time limit for care after the birth. Midwife help during the postpartum period ("Wochenbettbetreuung") is covered until 12 weeks after the birth ("bis zum Ablauf von zwölf Wochen nach der Geburt"). Anything beyond that requires a doctor's order ("weitergehende Leistungen bedürfen der ärztlichen Anordnung").

If the mother cannot care for the child after the birth, the insured child has its own entitlement to the midwife services that relate to the child.

If you are privately insured, the Familienportal says you should check with your insurer in advance which services it covers.

This is the general rule. Whether a particular service is covered in your case is decided by your Krankenkasse.

rows.question: How do we insure the baby after the birth?
rows.reply:
Under German statutory health insurance, a child of an insured member can be covered through Familienversicherung (free family cover for dependants). SGB V §10(1) says children of members are insured if they:
1. have their residence or habitual abode in Germany ("ihren Wohnsitz oder gewöhnlichen Aufenthalt im Inland haben");
2. are not compulsorily insured under § 5(1) nos. 1 to 8, 11 to 12, and are not voluntarily insured;
3. are not exempt from insurance or released from compulsory insurance;
4. are not self-employed as their main occupation; and
5. have no total income regularly above one seventh of the monthly reference amount under § 18 SGB IV.

Under §10(2), children are covered up to age 18; up to 23 if not working; up to 25 if in school, vocational training or a recognised voluntary year; and without an age limit if, because of a disability, they cannot support themselves.

There is one exclusion that matters for parents. Under §10(3), children are not covered if the parent who is the member's spouse or civil partner and related to the child is not a member of a health insurance fund ("nicht Mitglied einer Krankenkasse"), and that parent's total income regularly exceeds one twelfth of the annual earnings ceiling ("Jahresarbeitsentgeltgrenze") and is regularly higher than the member's income.

If the conditions are met through more than one member, for example both parents, the member chooses the health insurance fund (§10(5)). The member must report the insured child, with the details needed to run the family cover, to the responsible health insurance fund (§10(6)).

The birth certificate is needed to register the child with the health insurance fund. You must register the birth within 1 week at the registry office (Standesamt) responsible for the place of birth, which issues the birth certificate.

Whether your child meets these conditions is decided by the responsible health insurance fund, not by this service. The excerpts do not cover how to insure a child who does not qualify for family cover, for example through private insurance. Private insurance is outside what this product covers; ask the insurer concerned.

rows.question: When are the first check-ups for the baby?
rows.reply:
The Kinder-Richtlinie (the federal guideline on early detection of illness in children) sets out ten check-ups in the first six years of life, "insgesamt zehn Untersuchungen". They can only be used within set periods, each with a tolerance window ("Toleranzgrenze"). Each routine Vorsorgeuntersuchung (routine preventive check-up) is called a U-check: U1, U2 and so on.

The first ones fall in the baby's first year:
- U1: immediately after the birth ("Unmittelbar nach der Geburt"). It should take place within the first 30 minutes after the birth ("innerhalb der ersten 30 Minuten nach der Geburt"). The U1 has no tolerance window. If no doctor is present at the birth but a midwife is, the midwife should carry out the U1.
- U2: 3rd to 10th day of life. Tolerance window: 3rd to 14th day.
- U3: 4th to 5th week of life. Tolerance window: 3rd to 8th week.
- U4: 3rd to 4th month of life. Tolerance window: 2nd to 4½ months.
- U5: 6th to 7th month of life. Tolerance window: 5th to 8th month.
- U6: 10th to 12th month of life. Tolerance window: 9th to 14th month.

The later check-ups are:
- U7: 21st to 24th month. Tolerance window: 20th to 27th month.
- U7a: 34th to 36th month. Tolerance window: 33rd to 38th month.
- U8: 46th to 48th month. Tolerance window: 43rd to 50th month.
- U9: 60th to 64th month. Tolerance window: 58th to 66th month.

The same periods apply to babies born prematurely: "Auch bei Frühgeborenen sind die Untersuchungszeiträume einzuhalten." The premature birth is taken into account when the results are assessed.

The G-BA page for the guideline says the version currently offered came into force on 1 January 2026. It also says a decision that came into force on 20 August 2026 is not yet included in that version.

rows.question: What is Mutterschaftsgeld and when do I apply for it?
rows.reply:
Mutterschaftsgeld (maternity pay from the health insurer) is a payment for the protection periods before and after the birth ("die Zeit der Schutzfristen vor und nach der Entbindung") and for the day of the birth itself.

Who pays it depends on your insurance:

- If you are a member of a statutory health insurer, you receive Mutterschaftsgeld under the rules of the Fifth Book of the Social Code (SGB V) (MuSchG §19(1)).
- If you are not a member of a statutory health insurer, you receive Mutterschaftsgeld from federal funds, "jedoch insgesamt höchstens 210 Euro" (at most 210 euros in total). It is paid "auf Antrag" (on application) by the Bundesamt für Soziale Sicherung (MuSchG §19(2)).

Under SGB V §24i(1), female members of a health insurer receive it if either of these applies:

1. they are entitled to sickness benefit when unable to work, or
2. they are not paid wages because of the protection periods under §3 of the Maternity Protection Act.

It is also paid to women whose employment ends immediately before the protection period begins, if they were members of a health insurer on the last day of employment.

The amount for employed members is the net average daily pay of the last three settled calendar months before the protection period. It is "höchstens 13 Euro für den Kalendertag" (at most 13 euros per calendar day). If average pay is higher than 13 euros a day, the employer pays the difference as an employer supplement ("Zuschuss zum Mutterschaftsgeld") (SGB V §24i(2), MuSchG §20(1)). For other members, Mutterschaftsgeld is paid at the level of sickness benefit (SGB V §24i(2)). The claim is suspended while you receive pay that is subject to contributions. This does not apply to one-off payments (SGB V §24i(4)).

The protection periods normally begin 6 weeks before the calculated due date and end 8 weeks after the birth (familienportal.de).

On when to apply: the excerpts do not state a time limit or a date for applying. They state two things:

- For payment before the birth, the decisive document is a certificate from a doctor or midwife stating the expected day of delivery (SGB V §24i(3)).
- If your employment starts during the protection periods, Mutterschaftsgeld is paid from the start of employment (SGB V §24i(3)).

For how and when to apply, ask your statutory health insurer. If you are not statutorily insured, ask the Bundesamt für Soziale Sicherung.

Two related points:

- Mutterschaftsgeld under SGB V and the employer supplement under MuSchG §20 are counted against Elterngeld for the time from the day of birth. The 210-euro payment under MuSchG §19(2) is not counted (BEEG §3(1)).
- If you become pregnant again during parental leave and do not end that leave early, you can receive only the health insurer's Mutterschaftsgeld, not the employer supplement (familienportal.de).

Whether you qualify, and how much you would receive, is decided by your health insurer or, if you are not statutorily insured, by the Bundesamt für Soziale Sicherung.

rows.question: We are not married. Is my partner automatically the legal father?
rows.reply:
No. Under German law, being the child's biological father and living together does not by itself make your partner the legal father.

BGB §1592 says the father of a child is the man who:
1. is married to the child's mother at the time of the birth ("zum Zeitpunkt der Geburt mit der Mutter des Kindes verheiratet ist"),
2. has acknowledged paternity ("die Vaterschaft anerkannt hat"), or
3. has had his paternity established by a court ("gerichtlich festgestellt").

The first ground applies only to married parents. If the parents are not married at the birth, the father must make a Vaterschaftsanerkennung (acknowledgement of paternity) to count as the legal father. It is voluntary and needs the mother's consent.

How it is done:
- The father must make the declaration in person at a competent office. Examples are the youth welfare office, a registry office, a local court or a notary.
- The mother must also declare her consent in person.
- The office records both the father's declaration and the mother's consent.
- Depending on the federal state, acknowledgement at a notary or local court can cost a fee.
- Which documents are needed is explained on the federal portal (Bundesportal).

Rules on validity in BGB §1594:
- The acknowledgement can be made before the child is born ("schon vor der Geburt des Kindes zulässig").
- It has legal effect only from the moment it becomes effective.
- It is not effective while another man's paternity exists.
- An acknowledgement made subject to a condition or a time limit is invalid.
- It is not effective while court proceedings to establish another man's paternity are pending. The exception is a declaration made on the court's record under §180(2) of the Act on Proceedings in Family Matters.

If the mother is married to another man at the birth, that husband is the legal father and no acknowledgement can be made. The exception is a divorce petition filed before the birth. In that case acknowledgement is possible within one year after the divorce, with the consent of the mother and her husband, and it takes effect at the earliest when the divorce is final. The family portal notes that this information, and the information on court determination, is currently being updated because of a recent change in the law on challenging paternity.

If the father does not want to acknowledge, or the mother does not consent, the child, the mother or the presumed biological father can apply to a court to establish paternity.

Legal paternity does not automatically give custody. If the parents are not married at the birth, the mother has parental custody from the birth. For the father to share it, both parents must also declare that they want joint custody, or a court must decide it. Marrying after the birth also creates joint custody. Your local youth welfare office advises on parental custody.

This explains the general rule. The office that records the acknowledgement handles your own case.

rows.question: How do unmarried parents get joint custody?
rows.reply:
If the parents are not married to each other when the child is born, the mother has parental custody alone. BGB §1626a(3) says: "Im Übrigen hat die Mutter die elterliche Sorge."

BGB §1626a(1) gives three ways for unmarried parents to get joint custody:
1. Both parents declare that they want to take on custody jointly. These are called Sorgeerklärungen. A single declaration is a Sorgeerklärung (declaration of joint custody). The statute's words: "wenn sie erklären, dass sie die Sorge gemeinsam übernehmen wollen (Sorgeerklärungen)".
2. The parents marry each other: "wenn sie einander heiraten".
3. The family court transfers custody to both parents jointly: "soweit ihnen das Familiengericht die elterliche Sorge gemeinsam überträgt".

First, the father must be the legal father. The federal family portal explains that the other parent becomes the legal father in one of two ways:
- he recognises the child as his own with the mother's consent, or
- a court establishes paternity.

Recognising paternity does not by itself give custody. A Sorgeerklärung or a court decision is still needed.

The declarations are made, for example, at the youth welfare office or at a notary ("zum Beispiel beim Jugendamt oder bei einem Notar"). They can also be made before the birth ("Sorgeerklärungen können auch schon vor der Geburt abgegeben werden").

Under BGB §1626a(2), the family court acts on the application of one parent ("auf Antrag eines Elternteils"). It transfers all or part of custody to both parents jointly if this does not conflict with the child's welfare ("wenn die Übertragung dem Kindeswohl nicht widerspricht"). If the other parent gives no reasons against joint custody, and none are otherwise apparent, the law presumes that joint custody does not conflict with the child's welfare.

The family portal adds how this works in practice. The court sets a period within which reasons against joint custody can be raised. If none are raised, the court decides in a simplified procedure. In that procedure there is no hearing of the youth welfare office and no personal hearing of the parents.

Under SGB VIII §58(1), the competent youth welfare office keeps a custody register for children of unmarried parents. An entry is made in each of these cases:
1. Sorgeerklärungen under BGB §1626a(1) No. 1 are made.
2. A final court decision has transferred custody to the parents jointly, in whole or in part.
3. A final court decision has withdrawn custody from the mother, in whole or in part, or transferred it to the father alone.

Under SGB VIII §18(2), mothers and fathers who are not married to each other are entitled to advice on making a Sorgeerklärung and on the option of a court transfer of joint custody. Your local youth welfare office gives this advice. For a court transfer, the application goes to the family court.

rows.question: Will our baby automatically be German if we are both Indian citizens?
rows.reply:
Not automatically because you are Indian citizens. German law gives a child born to foreign parents German Staatsangehörigkeit (citizenship) at birth only if certain conditions are met.

Citizenship through a parent: under StAG §4(1), a child acquires German Staatsangehörigkeit at birth "wenn ein Elternteil die deutsche Staatsangehörigkeit besitzt", that is, if one parent is German.

Citizenship through birth in Germany: under StAG §4(3), a child of foreign parents born in Germany ("Durch die Geburt im Inland") acquires German Staatsangehörigkeit if one parent meets both of these conditions:
1. has lawfully had their habitual residence in Germany for five years ("seit fünf Jahren rechtmäßig seinen gewöhnlichen Aufenthalt im Inland"), and
2. holds an unlimited right of residence ("ein unbefristetes Aufenthaltsrecht"), or, as a Swiss citizen or a Swiss citizen's family member, a residence permit under the 1999 EU–Switzerland agreement on free movement.
The acquisition is entered in the birth register where the birth is recorded.

How this is checked: under PStV §34, when the birth is reported, the registry office ("das Standesamt") asks whether a parent holds an unlimited right of residence. If the answers indicate this, it obtains written information from the immigration authority ("der Ausländerbehörde") on whether the details are correct and whether that parent had five years of lawful habitual residence in Germany at the time of the birth. It also obtains this information, for both parents, if the parents give no details or the registry office doubts them. The registry office then examines whether the child acquired German Staatsangehörigkeit and records the result.

If the child does not become German: under AufenthG §33, a child born in Germany can be granted a residence permit ex officio if one parent holds an "Aufenthaltserlaubnis", a "Niederlassungserlaubnis" or an "Erlaubnis zum Daueraufenthalt – EU". If both parents, or the parent with sole custody, hold one of these at the time of birth, the child is granted the residence permit ex officio. If a parent holds a visa or may stay visa-free at the time of birth, the child's stay counts as permitted until that visa or visa-free stay ends.

Whether your child meets these conditions is not something this service can decide. The registry office where the birth is registered examines it, with information from your local immigration authority.

rows.question: Does our newborn need a residence permit?
rows.reply:
Whether a child born in Germany needs a residence permit depends on the parents' status at the time of birth. The law sets out these routes. Which one applies to your child is decided by the authorities, not here.

1. German citizenship at birth. A child acquires German citizenship at birth if one parent is a German citizen (StAG §4(1)). A child of foreign parents born in Germany also acquires German citizenship at birth if one parent both:
- has lawfully had their habitual residence in Germany for five years, and
- holds an unlimited right of residence ("unbefristetes Aufenthaltsrecht"), or, as a Swiss citizen or a Swiss citizen's family member, holds a residence permit under the 21 June 1999 free movement agreement between the European Community and Switzerland (StAG §4(3)).

This acquisition is entered in the birth register. When the birth is registered, the registry office asks whether a parent holds such a status. It obtains written information from the foreigners' authority on whether this is correct and whether the parent had five years of lawful habitual residence at the time of birth. The registry office then checks whether the child acquired German citizenship (PStV §34).

2. Aufenthaltserlaubnis (residence permit) for a child born in Germany (AufenthG §33):
- If one parent holds an Aufenthaltserlaubnis, a settlement permit or an EU long-term residence permit, the child "kann" (may) be granted an Aufenthaltserlaubnis ex officio.
- If, at the time of birth, both parents, or the parent with sole custody, hold one of these permits, the child "wird" (is) granted the Aufenthaltserlaubnis ex officio.
- If a parent holds a visa, or is allowed to stay without a visa, at the time of birth, the child's stay counts as permitted until that visa or visa-free stay expires.

The excerpts do not say which office issues the child's Aufenthaltserlaubnis, or what steps you take. Your local foreigners' authority is the office to approach about your child's residence status. The registry office that registers the birth carries out the citizenship check.

rows.question: We are getting Mutterschaftsgeld. Does that reduce our Elterngeld?
rows.reply:
Yes, as a general rule. The law sets out how Mutterschaftsgeld (maternity pay from the health insurer) interacts with Elterngeld (parental allowance). Only the Elterngeld office responsible for your district decides your own case and amount.

What is credited against Elterngeld. BEEG §3(1) lists income that is "auf das … Elterngeld … angerechnet" (credited against Elterngeld). This includes Mutterschaftsleistungen (maternity benefits) "in Form des Mutterschaftsgeldes nach dem Fünften Buch Sozialgesetzbuch" and "in Form des Zuschusses zum Mutterschaftsgeld nach § 20 des Mutterschutzgesetzes". Both count "für die Zeit ab dem Tag der Geburt des Kindes" (for the period from the day of the child's birth). The employer's top-up is set out in MuSchG §20.

The one exception. Mutterschaftsgeld under MuSchG §19(2) is not credited. That is the payment for women who are not members of a statutory health insurer. It is paid by the Bundesamt für Soziale Sicherung and is limited to "insgesamt höchstens 210 Euro" (at most 210 euros in total).

No protected minimum for the same child. BEEG §3(2) normally keeps the first 300 euros of Elterngeld free from crediting. It does not do so "soweit … Einnahmen nach Absatz 1 Satz 1 Nummer 1 bis 3" are credited, and maternity benefits fall under number 1. The federal Familienportal explains it this way. Maternity benefits for the same child are credited in full. If the maternity benefits are higher than the Elterngeld, only the maternity benefits are paid. If the Elterngeld is higher, the difference is paid as Elterngeld on top.

rows.question: Can I work while receiving Elterngeld?
rows.reply:
Yes, within a limit set by the law. Working does not by itself rule out Elterngeld (parental allowance), but it limits who qualifies and changes the amount.

The limit. One condition for Elterngeld is that the person "keine oder keine volle Erwerbstätigkeit ausübt" (does no work, or does not work full time) (BEEG §1(1) No. 4). The law says a person is not in full-time work if any of these three applies (BEEG §1(6)):
1. their working time does not exceed 32 hours a week on average over the child's month of life ("32 Wochenstunden im Durchschnitt des Lebensmonats");
2. they are in employment for vocational training ("Beschäftigung zur Berufsbildung");
3. they work as a suitable childminder under §§ 23 and 43 of Book VIII of the Social Code ("geeignete Kindertagespflegeperson").
People who are temporarily not working still count as working while they remain in an employment relationship or are self-employed (BEEG §1(6a)).

The effect on the amount. For months after the birth in which you earn less than before the birth, Elterngeld is paid as the applicable percentage of the difference between the two incomes. For this, income before the birth is counted up to at most 2,770 euros. The difference is calculated separately for months of basic Elterngeld and months of Elterngeld Plus (BEEG §2(3)). The maximum of 1,800 euros a month applies to full months with no income from work (BEEG §2(1)). Instead of one month of basic Elterngeld, a person can take two months of Elterngeld Plus (BEEG §4(3)). The federal family portal says Elterngeld Plus can be especially worthwhile when working part time, and that the partnership bonus may be of interest if both parents work part time at the same time.

What the application and proof involve. If the application states expected income from work during the payment period, the actual income must be proven after the period ends, and the amount is decided provisionally until then (BEEG §8(1), §8(3) No. 3). If the application says there will be no income from work, Elterngeld is paid subject to revocation if there is income after all (BEEG §8(2)). The family portal lists as proof an employer's certificate of working hours during the Elterngeld period, or, for self-employed people, their own declaration of their previous working hours and their hours during the Elterngeld period. It says the employer is obliged to issue the documents.

The family portal says its explanations apply to children born after August 2021, and that partly different rules apply to children born before 1 September 2021. Whether and how much Elterngeld you receive while working is decided by your "Elterngeldstelle", the Elterngeld office for your district. This answer does not assess your own case or calculate an amount.

rows.question: Where and how do we apply for Kindergeld?
rows.reply:
Where: the law says the application "soll bei der nach § 13 zuständigen Familienkasse gestellt werden" (BKGG §9(1)). BKGG §13(1) sets which Familienkasse that is. It is the one for the district where the claimant has their residence ("Wohnsitz"). If there is no residence in Germany, it is the one for the district of their habitual stay ("gewöhnlicher Aufenthalt"). If there is neither, it is the one for the district where they work ("erwerbstätig"). In all other cases it is the "Familienkasse Bayern Nord". The same Familienkasse receives the application and decides on the claim. The Familienportal says to apply to "der Familienkasse Ihrer Agentur für Arbeit", which is normally responsible for processing it.

How: Kindergeld (child benefit) must be applied for in writing: "schriftlich zu beantragen" (BKGG §9(1)). Besides the person entitled, anyone with a legitimate interest in the payment may also apply.

The Familienportal describes the practical steps:
- Apply electronically or in writing, using the Familienkassen's form.
- You can fill the form in online, then print it and sign it.
- For a newborn child, you can also apply fully online with a valid ELSTER certificate, with no printing or handwritten signature.
- You must give your own tax identification number and your child's tax identification number.
- If you have questions about applying, the Bundesagentur für Arbeit has a free service line: 0800 4 555530.

Who applies: for each child, only one person receives Kindergeld (BKGG §3(1)). If the child lives in the shared household of both parents, the parents decide between themselves who is the entitled person. If they do not decide, the family court decides on application (BKGG §3(2)).

Child born or living abroad: the Bundesagentur für Arbeit asks for a copy of the foreign birth certificate. Another official document certifying the birth can be used instead. Evidence can be sent online to your Familienkasse. If further documents are needed, the Familienkasse tells you by when. If you miss that date, the application may be delayed or refused.

Back payment: according to the Familienportal, Kindergeld can be paid for up to 6 months retroactively. This applies where it was due but not paid, for example because no application was made. To apply retroactively, state in the application that you are doing so and from when you want Kindergeld.

Whether you are entitled is decided by the responsible Familienkasse, not here.

rows.question: What are the Elterngeld rules for a self-employed parent in Bavaria?
rows.reply:
Bavaria is outside the states this product covers. It covers federal law and Hessen procedures only. For how and where to apply in Bavaria, contact the Elterngeld office responsible for your place of residence in Bavaria. The rules below are federal law (BEEG) and apply in every state, including Bavaria.

Who is entitled (BEEG §1(1)). A person has a claim to Elterngeld (parental allowance) if they:
1. have a residence or habitual abode in Germany,
2. live in one household with the child,
3. care for and raise the child themselves, and
4. do not work, or do not work full time.

Under §1(6), a person is not working full time if:
1. their working time does not exceed 32 hours a week on average in the month of the child's life,
2. they are in employment for vocational training, or
3. they work as a qualified childminder.

Under §1(6a), self-employed people who are temporarily not working still count as working ("selbständig erwerbstätig").

The claim lapses if the person's taxable income in the last completed tax assessment period before the birth was more than 175,000 euros. Where another person also qualifies, the limit applies to both persons' combined taxable income (§1(8)).

Self-employment income counts (BEEG §2(1)). Income from work includes positive income from "Land- und Forstwirtschaft, Gewerbebetrieb und selbständiger Arbeit" (agriculture and forestry, trade or business, and self-employed work), taxable in Germany, after deductions for tax and social contributions. §2(1) says this income is calculated under §§2c to 2f. Of those, only §2c is among the excerpts, and §2c covers income from employment, not self-employment. The excerpts therefore do not show how self-employed income is determined in detail.

Amounts (BEEG §2):
- Elterngeld is 67 percent of income from work before the birth. It is capped at 1,800 euros a month for months with no income from work (§2(1)).
- If pre-birth income was below 1,000 euros, the percentage rises by 0.1 points for every 2 euros below 1,000, up to 100 percent. If it was above 1,200 euros, the percentage falls by 0.1 points for every 2 euros above 1,200, down to 65 percent (§2(2)).
- If you earn less after the birth than before, Elterngeld is the applicable percentage of the difference. Pre-birth income counts up to at most 2,770 euros for this (§2(3)).
- The minimum is 300 euros, even with no income from work before the birth (§2(4)).

Provisional decisions and proof (BEEG §8). These rules matter where income depends on a tax assessment.

Under §8(3), the amount is decided provisionally, based on the information you have made credible, if:
1. the tax assessment ("Steuerbescheid") for the last completed assessment period before the birth is not yet available and it cannot yet be said whether the §1(8) limits are exceeded,
2. income from work before the birth cannot be determined, or
3. the application states you are expected to have income from work during the payment period.

Where the application gave expected income, actual income for that period must be proved after the payment period ends (§8(1)). Payments are made subject to revocation in two cases (§8(2)):
- if you stated you expect no income from work but in fact have some, or
- if the tax assessment is missing and the limits under §1(8) turn out to be exceeded.

Duration (BEEG §4). Elterngeld is paid as basic Elterngeld or as Elterngeld Plus, in monthly amounts for months of the child's life.
- Parents together have 12 monthly amounts of basic Elterngeld.
- They get 2 more if one parent's income from work is reduced for two months.
- One month of basic Elterngeld can be taken as two months of Elterngeld Plus.
- A parent must draw Elterngeld for at least two months.
- Longer periods apply for children born at least six, eight, twelve or 16 weeks early (§4(5)).

Other income (BEEG §3). Some other payments are offset against Elterngeld. These are maternity benefits, comparable foreign benefits, Elterngeld for an older child, and income that replaces earnings.

Whether you qualify and how much you would receive is decided only by the responsible Elterngeld office, not here.

rows.question: Based on our situation, will our Elterngeld application be approved?
rows.reply:
Whether your application will be approved is decided only by the Elterngeld office (Elterngeldstelle) responsible for your district. This service cannot assess your situation or predict the outcome. Below is what the law says.

Basic conditions (BEEG §1(1)). A person is entitled to Elterngeld (parental allowance) if they:
1. have their residence or usual place of stay in Germany;
2. live in one household with the child;
3. look after and bring up the child themselves; and
4. work not at all, or not full time.
For twins or other multiple births there is only one entitlement.

"Not full time" (BEEG §1(6)) means any one of these:
1. working no more than "32 Wochenstunden" (32 hours a week) on average in the month of the child's life;
2. being in vocational training; or
3. working as a suitably qualified childminder under §§23 and 43 SGB VIII.

Conditions for non-EU nationals (BEEG §1(7)). A foreign national without EU free-movement rights is entitled only if they hold one of these:
1. a settlement permit or an EU long-term residence permit;
2. an EU Blue Card, an ICT card, a Mobile ICT card, or a residence permit that allows, or allowed, work for at least six months. The statute excludes some permits from this: training, au pair, seasonal work, European Voluntary Service or job-seeking permits; study, qualification-recognition or job-seeking permits where the person is not working, not on parental leave and not receiving SGB III benefits; and certain humanitarian permits;
3. one of those humanitarian permits, while lawfully working, on parental leave or receiving SGB III benefits;
4. one of those humanitarian permits, after at least 15 months of permitted, authorised or tolerated stay in Germany; or
5. a Beschäftigungsduldung (toleration for employment) under §60d AufenthG.
Minors are entitled under point 3 regardless of work.

Income limit (BEEG §1(8)). There is no entitlement if taxable income in the last completed tax year before the birth was "mehr als 175 000 Euro" (more than 175,000 euros). Where another person also qualifies, for example the other parent in the household, the limit applies to the two incomes added together.

Applying (BEEG §7(1)). Elterngeld must be applied for in writing ("schriftlich zu beantragen"). It is paid back only for the last three months of the child's life before the month the application arrives. Applying later loses the earlier months.

Documents. The federal family portal lists the child's birth certificate and proof of your previous income. Further documents may be needed depending on the case.

If you disagree with a decision. The family portal says an objection (Widerspruch) against the Elterngeld decision must be made in writing to your Elterngeld office within one month of receiving it.

For a decision on your own case, contact the Elterngeld office for your district in Hessen.

rows.question: How much tax will we save if I switch to Steuerklasse 3 before the birth?
rows.reply:
How much tax a switch to tax class III would save you is a tax calculation for your household. This service cannot work that out or say whether switching is worthwhile. Only a tax adviser (Steuerberater) or your local tax office (Finanzamt) can advise on your tax class choice and its tax effects.

The excerpts do cover how a tax class change before the birth affects the separate calculation of Elterngeld:

- A change of tax class before the birth "kann sich ... auf die Höhe Ihrer Steuern und Ihrer Sozialabgaben auswirken" (can affect the amount of your taxes and social contributions).
- For the simplified "Elterngeld-Netto", the newest tax class counts. The older tax class is used only if it applied for longer than the newer one within the whole assessment period ("Bemessungszeitraum"). The same applies to other deduction features, such as the number of child allowances.
- For employment income, the assessment period is "die zwölf Kalendermonate vor dem Kalendermonat der Geburt des Kindes" (the twelve calendar months before the month of birth). BEEG §2b(1) leaves out months in which the person:
  1. received Elterngeld for an older child within the periods it specifies;
  2. could not be employed during the maternity protection periods, or received maternity benefit or the sickness daily allowance it names;
  3. had an illness mainly caused by the pregnancy; or
  4. performed military or civilian service.
  These months are counted instead if the person applies for that.
- The income tax deduction is set using your tax class and, where relevant, the factor under § 39f of the Income Tax Act. Tax class VI is disregarded.
- Changing tax class again after the birth no longer has any effect on Elterngeld.

The "Elterngeldstelle" calculates the Elterngeld-Netto from your gross income and decides your Elterngeld. For the tax side of your question, contact a Steuerberater or your Finanzamt.
